strengths: Novel rigorous characterization of chaos in high-dimensional gradient descent, extending beyond prior univariate analyses
Technically sound mathematical framework with precise theorems, elegant quotient dynamics reduction, and multiple perspectives on chaos (topological entropy, fractals, sensitivity)
Comprehensive treatment including regularized/unregularized cases, identity initialization, and well-executed experiments demonstrating fractal structure and dimension estimation
Interesting negative results including non-existence of continuous dynamical invariants under large step sizes
Clear and well-organized presentation with effective visualizations and reproducible code
weaknesses: Critical limitation: Main theoretical results only proven for initialization subspace W with d ≥ d_y; general initializations treated only experimentally, severely restricting the claimed scope
Incomplete extension from scalar to matrix factorization—Proposition 5 is informal and covering map mechanism is heuristic rather than rigorously proven
Questionable practical relevance: near-critical step sizes are impractical, most training uses adaptive methods, and paper doesn't explain why practitioners should care about this chaotic regime
Measure-theoretic 'almost everywhere' statements obscure practical initialization sensitivity; unstable minimizers have measure-zero basins but remain physically visible
Limited insights into mechanisms: paper doesn't characterize what implicit bias replaces the non-existent simple ones (balance, minimum norm), or how to avoid pathological behavior
Fractal dimension 1.249 is numerically estimated rather than analytically proven; gap between scalar analysis and matrix case transfer not fully justified

strengths: Novel theoretical contribution: First rigorous characterization of fractal convergence boundaries in gradient descent for matrix factorization with exact critical step size analysis
Rigorous mathematical analysis using sophisticated dynamical systems theory (quotient dynamics, topological entropy, Lyapunov functions) with comprehensive proofs
Interesting geometric insights: Discovery that convergence region exhibits fractal structure with dimension ~1.249 is genuinely novel and connects GD to classical chaos theory
Comprehensive scope: Results cover unregularized and regularized problems, scalar and general matrix factorization, and extensions to neural networks
Strong empirical validation: Clear visual correspondence between theoretical predictions and experiments, including validation on real neural networks (CIFAR-10, deep ReLU)
Well-organized presentation with clear motivation, precise theorem statements, and pedagogical progression from simple to complex settings
Rigorous technical treatment: Proofs appear sound and employ appropriate mathematical machinery; analysis of convergence region geometry is thorough
weaknesses: Limited practical relevance: Theory focuses on near-critical step sizes where chaos emerges, but practitioners use smaller step sizes; practical implications and when to apply these insights remain unclear
Theory-practice gap: Theoretical results are primarily for matrix factorization but experiments include deep networks; connection between the two settings could be more explicit and rigorous
Scope limitations: Main results focus on scalar factorization initially; extension to general matrix factorization requires restrictive orthogonal initialization assumption

Phenomenon not entirely novel: Prior work (Kong & Tao 2020, Chen et al. 2024) already documented chaos at large step sizes; novelty lies primarily in the geometric characterization rather than discovery of chaos itself

Limited discussion of implications: Paper shows chaotic behavior exists but doesn't adequately discuss how this relates to generalization, implicit regularization, or when practitioners should be concerned about these phenomena
Experimental limitations: Deep network experiments validate phenomena but don't fully verify matrix factorization theory predictions; limited comparison with alternative theoretical frameworks
Restrictive assumptions for extensions: General matrix factorization (Section 4.1) requires orthogonal initializations; results for regularized problems require specific parametrization
Missing practical guidance: No discussion of how to detect or avoid chaotic regimes in practice, or whether these phenomena have implications for modern optimization
